description: Every row of the Essai's reuse tables that the first readers rated possible, read by a second reader (Claude Opus, tools/transcription/VERIFY_PROMPT_ESSAI.md): right, weak or wrong, and whether the label fits.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff notes that 'jus' is commonly taken for 'lex'; the confusion of law and right in common speech is a commonplace (Hobbes, Pufendorf), and Vattel's three-way distinction adds Morale.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition, natural laws as those 'que nous tenons de la Nature' whose reason lies in the essence and nature of man and things, renders Wolff §§ 135-136 (law of nature constituted by that essence and nature).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'science pratique' that teaches how to direct our faculties to do good and avoid evil follows Wolff's § 2 definition of practical science as the science of directing the faculties to acts carried out or omitted according to will and nill.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: A broader moral science covering natural law and ethics is a stock division; Wolff's genus is 'philosophia practica' with four disciplines, so even if the link held this would be a shared division, not a paraphrase.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff §§ 281–284 argue from God's wisdom that God cannot prescribe a law other than the one posited by human essence and nature, and that voluntarists end up at the same law; Vattel § 8 makes the same argument in Wolff's terms.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff § 284 makes the same argument: God's will tends to the best, so those who ground natural law in his will must reach the direction of actions deduced from man's nature, as Vattel's 'même source' says.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'convenance ou disconvenance des actions avec cette essence & avec cette nature' renders Wolff's actions 'essentiae & naturae nostrae convenientes/disconvenientes', with Wolff's essence-and-nature pairing (Wolff cited at §6).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel only lists the superior's-authority view among others; Wolff § 131 criticises that school's definition of law, a diagnosis the passage does not take up.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The call for clear and distinct ideas and good definitions is a Wolffian commonplace; Wolff § 188 makes the narrower complaint that conformity with human nature is not explained distinctly.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both say the authors' opposition over the principle is only apparent and comes from bad method, but Wolff's ground is demonstrative interdependence (the parabola); Vattel's is neglected definitions, and it concerns the principle of obligation.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both set moral beside physical necessity, but Vattel's definition (what an intelligent being's nature cannot fail to produce) is not Wolff's (whose opposite is morally impossible).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Direction of free actions and their rectitude are pervasive Wolffian terms; §114 uses them in a passing scholium on harmony of actions, not as a definition of duty, so the link to this passage is not shown.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's remark that the sufficient-reason definition 'revient à' the convenance/disconvenance of actions with man's nature as foundation of natural law is Wolff's § 188 reconciliation with Grotius's convenientia.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's object of self-love, 'la perfection de notre état, tant interne qu'externe', is Wolff's 'perfectio nostra statusque nostri', which § 104 declares desirable for its own sake.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'perfection de notre état, tant interne qu'externe', split into soul, body and fortune, follows Wolff's division of human perfection by soul, body and external state.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'vraie définition' of the useful (what truly contributes to the perfection of soul, body and our state in this world) restates Wolff's 'bonum verum' as what really promotes the perfection of ourselves and our state.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That we act only for some perceived good is the scholastic commonplace; Wolff's §105 deals with per se desirable actions, and the shared premise does not show this passage is Vattel's source.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's 'utilité réelle ou apparente' uses the commonplace real/apparent good distinction; Wolff's §75 makes a different point (a true good regarded as apparent because of sensual pleasure).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff pairs intrinsic goodness and God's attributes as the virtuous man's motives, but ranking love of God and of virtue above fear and fortune is a common theme; Wolff gives no ranking of this kind.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That man needs others and that society is necessary to a happy life is a commonplace of sociability, and Wolff's 'no one can perfect himself alone' shares no specific wording or argument with Vattel's sentence.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: 'Ce motif fait l'obligation' applies Wolff's definition of active obligation as the connection of a motive with an action (§118, which Vattel cites at §12).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The move from self-interest plus need of others to social duty is common stock (Pufendorf's imbecillitas, Hobbes); Vattel argues from utility and society's general rules, not from Wolff's joint pursuit of perfection.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff's concession that men founding civil societies made laws out of utility is a commonplace answer to Carneades, and Vattel's account of why men entered society and made laws shares no specific wording or sequence with it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's evil action 'contraire à ... la perfection de votre être' is Wolff's definition of the evil action as one tending to our imperfection.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's two grounds for the superior's will (1° obedience to a legitimate superior is itself laudable, 2° rewards and punishments the action does not bring by itself) match Wolff's split between the natural obligation to obey a superior and positive obligation through sanctions.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's second ground, rewards and punishments added 'indépendamment du bien ou du mal que notre action entraîne naturellement', is Wolff's positive obligation, good or evil joined to an action 'quod ex ea per se non sequitur'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 302: in positive obligation the legislator freely joins whatever reward or penalty he wills to an action not good in itself; Vattel says of the indifferent action that God may attach any reward he pleases.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both tie God's will in the natural law to what reason shows, but Wolff's identity of living by reason and by God's will is not Vattel's specific point that without seen reasons we cannot know God's will, and the idea is common stock.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff's atheist hypothesis and Vattel's obligation apart from God's will share the Grotian etiamsi daremus thesis; Vattel's wording comes from Barbeyrac's note and nothing ties it to § 245.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's reply follows Wolff §§ 273-274: deriving natural law from the nature of man and things takes nothing from God's legislative authority ('nihil derogari', 'non adimi potestatem legislatoriam').

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's utility, lying in observing order and virtue because they make us more perfect, is the Wolffian argument of § 263 that natural law is useful because it promotes our perfection.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That the atheist keeps some natural duties is a topos (Grotius, Leibniz, Bayle). Vattel is defending Leibniz's own text with his own grounds (this-life utility, beauty of virtue), where Wolff's limit is the lack of duties to God.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff §§ 251-252 derives the obligation to act on motives drawn from the divine attributes from the nature of God and man, not from God's will; Vattel's middle way (God among the 'choses' whose nature supplies the obliging motives) is the same specific move.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's reply that the nature of things obliges because its bearing on our happiness supplies a motive is Wolff's argument (§§ 127-128) that man's and things' nature, by joining motives to actions, obliges in the proper sense.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Wolff's pious man takes his motive from God's will, but Vattel's specific point (God's will moves us when we cannot see an action's intrinsic reasons) is not in § 341.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac stipulates a broad 'Morale' that includes droit naturel; Vattel notes such everyday confusion and then distinguishes the terms, so there is only a shared premise (both guide conduct), with no sign that he has this sentence in view.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both reply that a law invented for utility must still rest on nature, but Vattel's argument (knowing what is useful requires nature) differs from Epicurus's in Pufendorf (each naturally wants his good).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf's remark that natural-law principles are found by considering man's nature is a stock claim; Vattel speaks of utility-inventors, and nothing specific links him to II.3.14.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note (Buddeus on voluntarists' uncertainty whether God commands a law or its contrary, followed by Barbeyrac's point that such a law could only be known through the nature of things) carries the argument Vattel uses: they can know which laws God gave only by considering nature.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: 'Avantageux ... en général & ... en particulier' is a stock French doublet; Pufendorf's Epicurean argument (justice invented for the common good) is not Vattel's argument about God's wise laws, so at most a verbal echo.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both quote Cicero's dictum, but Vattel's 'Naturâ ipsâ constitutum est jus' follows Wolff § 136 ('Ipsa natura ... constitutum jus est') after the same argument; a shared ancient tag.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Astreint par une nécessité morale' is the stock juristic definition of obligation (Inst. 3.13 'necessitate adstringimur'); Vattel's analysis of ordinary usage is closer to Burlamaqui and does not point to Pufendorf in particular.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's account of obligation (astreints, liés, not forced physically but moved morally, through motives that bend the will) follows Pufendorf I.6.5's contrast of obligation acting morally with a physical push; Vattel quotes this paragraph's note n.4 in §§26-27.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's two possible answers to why one obeys a superior (the obedience is just, or he can punish) are Pufendorf's two grounds of authority in DNG I.6.9 (just reasons and power to harm), addressed to Barbeyrac, who follows him.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: In §18 (referred back to in §27, where he quotes this same note I.6.5 n.4) Vattel answers Barbeyrac's claim that the motive and the foundation of obligation are joined but must not be confused: the motives 'joints' to obedience are the obligation.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That self-love is the strongest inclination is a commonplace; Vattel's version (primitive desire for perfection of soul, body and fortune) is Wolffian, not Pufendorf's.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the scholastic axiom that we desire only what we judge good or useful (real or apparent), a common doctrine; Vattel's soul, body and fortune scheme is Wolffian.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The real/apparent good distinction is a scholastic commonplace; nothing beyond it links Vattel's sentence to this Barbeyrac note.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The words 'passent avec raison pour les plus nobles' match, but it is an ordinary idiom, and Pufendorf applies it to acts done for others' utility, Vattel to motives tied to the soul's perfection.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's thesis that utility is the first principle of all obligation is exactly what this note condemns; he quotes the note in full in § 30 and defends the utility principle against it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note does separate sociability as the principle of social duties from the foundation of obligation, but that split was standard after Barbeyrac; Vattel's own first-vs-proximate wording is absent from the note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's grounding of the duty to keep social laws in each one's own utility matches the reading Barbeyrac reports from Titius, but nothing in the wording points to this note rather than the common Pufendorfian sociability-from-need argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's E.24–25 argument (sacrifice a present advantage to the general rules that secure lasting goods, repose and safety) follows DNG II.3.10's reason-versus-passion utility and its sequel; Vattel quotes the same paragraph's note 6 and its Cicero/Socrates in § 30.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both hold that a society serving self-interest obliges one sometimes to put the public before one's particular advantage, a commonplace; Vattel's reason, that the rules secure the enjoyment of all one's goods, is absent.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel answers this very note (L. I c. vi § 5 n. 4, named in E.26-27) and openly embraces the grounding of obligation in utility that Barbeyrac condemns there as reducing everything to one's own utility.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: 'Tient lieu de raison' renders Juvenal's tag, which Vattel takes from Wolff § 132 as he says; Pufendorf uses it of a legislator's free departure from general reason in interpreting laws.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel grants Barbeyrac's general thesis that the thought of God has great 'efficace'; the shared word and concession are too common to tie the sentence to Préface § 6 in particular.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel quoted this note's motive/ground distinction at § 27. Here, answering Barbeyrac, he corrects it: the idea of God acts only as a motive, and its obliging force comes from our felicity.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: The thesis Vattel calls a begging of the question, that all obligation comes from an external principle, a superior's will, is Pufendorf's DNG I.6.7-8 doctrine, down to 'principe externe' and 'Supérieur'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition takes the preface's frame: natural law as the most general duties of man as man (as against citizen and Christian), the rules of what he must do or not do.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's narrow sense of Morale covers internal movements as opposed to external acts, while Vattel's covers duties to oneself as opposed to duties to others. The distinctions differ and only the topic is shared.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both tie natural law to what others 'ont droit d'exiger', but Barbeyrac is making a point about external acts, not drawing Vattel's Morale/Droit Naturel distinction, and the phrase is common.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's two questions (foundation and principle of obligation) frame the general dispute; Barbeyrac's gloss on Leibniz's efficient cause addresses only obligation, and the distinction is common.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the phrase 'la beauté même de la vertu' is shared: Barbeyrac speaks of it as the noblest motive to duty, not as one school's ground of obligation, so the content is not paraphrased.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: E.11 states Vattel's own account of motives overriding the heart's inclination; it does not take up Barbeyrac's claim, which Vattel quotes and answers only at E.38.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Barbeyrac does make acting by duty the ground of moral necessity, but Vattel presents 'le devoir fait l'obligation' as a common way of speaking with no echo tying it to Réflexions § 16.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's is the stock definition of duty, but Vattel's wording ('action déterminée ... en tant que nous sommes obligés à la déterminer') translates Wolff PPU § 224, not Pufendorf.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's summary of Barbeyrac's notes on Pufendorf (obligation as dependence on a superior who 'nous assujettit') restates this note's 'Etre qui ait droit de nous assujettir à suivre certaines régles'.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Réflexions § 16 makes moral necessity consist in conforming to the will one depends on; Vattel, naming Barbeyrac, rejects exactly this identification of obligation with dependence and submission.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel asks whether Barbeyrac (named) will say obedience is due because it is just, which is Barbeyrac's answer in Réflexions § 19 (authority founded on reasons of justice), and rejects it as a motive.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Self-love leading us to seek our good is a commonplace; the shared 'qui ... porte ... à' construction is not specific enough to tie Vattel to Devoirs I.5.1.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Obeying God out of something other than fear is a commonplace; Vattel's passing ranking of motives shares only 'indépendamment de toute crainte' with Barbeyrac (and with Pufendorf I.6.9).

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's inference from utility as primitive motive to utility as first principle of obligation does contradict Barbeyrac's motive/ground split, but § 22 states the thesis without taking up Barbeyrac, who is answered only from § 27 on.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That observing natural law serves the observer's good is a commonplace; Vattel derives it from his own §§3 and 6, and nothing ties the sentence to Leibniz's §20 formula beyond the general idea.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The premise that man cannot subsist or enjoy his goods without society is the common Pufendorfian sociability argument; Vattel's distinctive step (obligation from one's own utility) is not in I.3.7.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The only link is the common idiom 'sans balancer' and the commonplace of putting the public good before private advantage; Vattel's reason (the rules secure his other goods) is not in Pufendorf's portrait of the good citizen.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That the legislator's will obliges even when the reason of the law is unseen is a stock maxim (stat pro ratione voluntas, which Vattel cites via Wolff); Pufendorf states it in passing in a chapter on interpretation.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel points to Barbeyrac's 'deux pages suivantes', which are exactly this passage on utility in this life and the beauty of virtue as a motive apart from future rewards, the point he makes for the atheist.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: The 'direz-vous' reply voices Barbeyrac's claim in Réflexions § 15, the paragraph Vattel is answering, that reason shows God wills us to follow reason, and Vattel turns it against him.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: In a paragraph answering Barbeyrac by name, Vattel takes up the afterlife consideration that Réflexions § 6 treats as a motive distinct from the ground of obligation, and corrects him: the idea of God acts only as a motive, and that motive is what obliges.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius-Barbeyrac's sentence is about justifying causes, motives and occasions of war; the only link is a stock phrase about terms being confused in ordinary language.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note, quoted by Vattel at E.29, concedes that the rules are deduced from relations in the nature of things while denying that this obliges; E.6-7 takes up exactly that sense of 'fondement' as what all authors must grant.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Following an a priori argument with an a posteriori confirmation is common method (Wolff's 'patet a posteriori ... experientia' is closer), and Vattel's appeal to experience is not Grotius's a posteriori proof from the consent of nations.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both reject utility as the source of natural law in favour of human nature, but this anti-Carneades answer was common stock; Vattel's argument and wording (utility is known only through the essence and nature of things) are Wolffian, not Grotius's.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Convenance ou disconvenance' of actions with nature is the Grotian formula in Barbeyrac's French, but by 1747 it was stock (Wolff, Barbeyrac, Burlamaqui), and Vattel's 'nature de l'homme & des choses' is Wolff's version, not Grotius's 'nature raisonnable & sociable'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note describes his opponents' appeal to the beauty of actions, but Vattel's 'beauté de la vertu' as a ground of obligation is a stock label for that school, with no wording that ties it to this note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel quotes this sentence later (§ 29), but the general claim in § 10 that undefined terms make authors only seem opposed is a stock diagnosis, not specific to Barbeyrac's remark about a dispute of words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac renders 'rectum' as 'bon & louable', but Vattel's gloss of rectitudo with stock synonyms (and its moralitas sentence) follows Wolff; the overlap is two ordinary words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Convenance ou disconvenance' of actions with nature is Grotius's stock definition, repeated everywhere; Vattel restates his own § 6, framed in Wolff's terms (essence and nature of man and things).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That utility goes along with natural law is Grotius's dictum but also a commonplace (Wolff § 263, Pufendorf). Vattel's 'jointe' shares only the idea, and his reason for it is his own.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Grotius's definition in Barbeyrac's French: actions prescribed or forbidden as a consequence of their 'convenance ou disconvenance' with our nature (Grotius: 'par conséquent' God 'ordonne ou défend').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius as making sociability the foundation of natural law, which is Grotius's claim at DP §8; the shared wording with Barbeyrac's note is only the stock attribution, so the row holds as a citation, not as a paraphrase of the note.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The Horace line with the same reference is a stock tag of the utility debate, also quoted by Pufendorf II.3.10 (whose lower-case spelling Vattel matches), and Vattel endorses it where Grotius rejects it. The shared quotation does not show Grotius as the source.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel quotes this note 4 in § 29 and answers its 'accessoire' objection there; § 35 (citing § 29) restates his answer: God's will only adds great weight to the reason drawn from the nature of things.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel concedes and then corrects the claim that relations of convenance only oblige us to recognise them, which this Grotius note states in nearly the same words, though his quotation follows the Réflexions.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's reply (reason shows that following these ideas serves our greatest good) is the very answer Barbeyrac anticipates and rejects in note 4 ('direz-vous'); § 39 quotes the identical Réflexions version and says 'M. B. a prévû cette réponse'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: It is the same Barbeyrac sentence ('n'est-il pas libre à chacun de renoncer à ...'). Vattel quotes the Réflexions version word for word, and this Grotius note has it in near-identical words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel quotes Barbeyrac's argument nearly word for word, the second clause verbatim; he takes it from the Réflexions but says in § 29 that note 4's proof is identical 'mot pour mot'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Anonyme, ou de (feu) Mr. de Leibniz' is Barbeyrac's standing formula, repeated in several notes including the Pufendorf note Vattel cites at E.26, so nothing ties it to this Grotius note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui says common language confuses 'volontaire' and 'libre'; Vattel that it confuses natural laws, natural right and morality, so only a generic remark and a stock notion of Morale are shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel says laws of nature, natural law and morals are often confused and must be distinguished; Burlamaqui defines a different triad (with jurisprudence naturelle) with different definitions and no claim of confusion.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Defining morals as what teaches us to bring our conduct into line with the rules of good and evil is a stock definition.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both want natural law to cover more than Pufendorf's mutual duties, but this is a common Barbeyrac-derived criticism, and Burlamaqui's sentence speaks of all of man's states, not of duties to oneself.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That writers disagree on the first principle of obligation is a generic transition, worded independently. Burlamaqui's sentence is closer to Vattel's § 10 than to this passage.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both say the foundation of natural law is to be sought nowhere else than in nature ('ne ... chercher ... ailleurs que dans') and that this explains why the laws are as they are.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared phrase 'convenance ou disconvenance' of actions with man's nature is Grotius's stock formula, used by Burlamaqui for a different point (the object of obligatory natural law).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Laws found by reason from man's nature forming the 'corps' of natural law is a stock definition, and Vattel defines droit naturel otherwise (E.3, a science of duties), so nothing points to Burlamaqui's definition.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both put confusion about obligation down to poor definitions, but Vattel's sentence is a general rule of method; the specific charge against Barbeyrac comes only at E.18 and E.27.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both define obligation by starting from what ordinary speakers mean and arrive at the same sequence: a moral, not physical, necessity, a bond ('lié') produced by motives or reasons that determine the will.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both explain obligation from common usage as moral, not physical, necessity produced by motives that bind the will ('puissans motifs ... liens' / 'liaison d'un motif puissant').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared phrase 'nécessité morale d'agir ou de ne pas agir' is Wolff's stock definition of passive obligation (§118), which both render; Burlamaqui's sentence, on imputation, does not share Vattel's sentence structure.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both tie moral necessity to motives that determine the will, but this is the common Wolffian doctrine (Wolff § 118, cited by Vattel) worded differently.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both define morality as a relation of free actions to a rule, but Burlamaqui refers it to law and Vattel (after Wolff § 134) to rectitude; only the defining form is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The 'first, primitive principle of obligation' is the standard framing of the debate. Burlamaqui's sentence opens a survey of opinions (closer to Vattel E.10), while E.19 sets Vattel's own requirement of one general motive from which all others derive.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both reduce competing principles of morality and obligation to a single general principle tied to happiness, using the same image of branches from a 'source commune'.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both treatises, while grounding obligation, hold that a reason or motive moves the will only by engaging our desire for good or happiness, and both use this to reduce rival principles to interest.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Preferring the good of the soul to that of the body, derived from the desire of happiness, is common doctrine; Burlamaqui uses it to derive duties to oneself, Vattel to define utility.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That natural laws suit our nature and so bring our happiness is a common eudaemonist claim; Vattel argues it from his own §§ 3 and 6 with nothing specific shared with Burlamaqui.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That society is natural and even necessary to a happy life is a natural-law commonplace; Burlamaqui's list of goods lost outside society adds nothing specific to Vattel's clause.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Burlamaqui makes sociability the principle of duties toward others, a post-Barbeyrac commonplace; Vattel's own point, that it is only the proximate and not the first principle of obligation, is not in Burlamaqui.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That a rational being cannot act against or be indifferent to its own happiness is a commonplace; the two texts share the idea, but nothing more specific than 'contradiction'/'absurde'.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both define obligation as a reason (or motive) that determines us to act in one way in preference to another, in largely shared words. This is a shared definition close enough in wording to count as a paraphrase.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Burlamaqui I.vi.9-11 runs Gastrell's whole sequence (obligation as a reason determining one way of acting over another, which moves the will only as a good to gain or evil to avoid, rival accounts reducing to it), and the clause has the same 'cette raison ... ne ... que ... acquérir / éviter' build.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both answer Barbeyrac by asking what grounds the duty to obey a superior, but this is the stock Leibnizian objection (Burlamaqui cites the Jugement § 15) and they resolve it differently (reason's approval, utility).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The union of power, wisdom and goodness as the basis of a superior's right is common Leibniz-Barbeyrac stock, and the two texts use it for different points (the right to command, against trusting a will whose reasons we cannot see).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both say God's will is known from the utility or necessity of duties, but Burlamaqui is ranking conflicting duties and Vattel contrasting natural with revealed law; no shared wording.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both reproduce Barbeyrac's sentence that reason does not put us in 'une nécessité indispensable de suivre' the ideas of fitness, with the same structure and most of the same words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both report Barbeyrac's conclusion that the maxims of reason are not obligatory without a superior's will, in nearly the same words, and both go on to reject it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The two answer different Barbeyrac arguments (Vattel the proof from believers' motives, Burlamaqui the no-self-obligation objection) and share only a stock charge of begging the question, whose real parallel is Essai § 40.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both defend the thesis that natural laws would bind without God's command against the charge that it excludes or derogates from God's will, in the same anti-Barbeyrac defence of Grotius.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both point to Leibniz's Jugement and Barbeyrac's reply and are cool toward Barbeyrac's defence, but the passages share only the reference to this well-known exchange, not wording or a specific argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes the same Barbeyrac thesis from Réflexions § 15 and, like Vattel, rejects it by making reason oblige through what leads to our felicity.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both say that reasons are felt too weakly against passion and that a further motive from the superior is needed, but this is the standard case for sanctions; Burlamaqui applies it to sovereignty and punishment and lacks Vattel's point about acting on God's will without seeing the reasons.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both explain the force of God's will as a motive through our interest in the superior's favour, a common eudaemonist point with no shared wording beyond 'déterminer'.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both argue that a being indifferent to its own happiness or misery could be forced by a superior power but never properly obliged, the same specific argument.
